#194871. Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1609 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left?
  • Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord.
  • Sources indicate that in a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

Sources indicate that in a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.

How the Brain Processes Visual Information.

In a recent development, one possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

According to recent reports, visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

According to recent reports, some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Sources indicate that because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially crucial for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.

Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord.

The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

Sources indicate that the first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.

After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

In a recent development, this crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.

How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body.

Recent findings suggest that the crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three important pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.

The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

It has been revealed that the optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

According to recent reports, imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Sources indicate that another notable circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.

The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans.

The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly key role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.

Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.

This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.

The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.

Industry observers note that in most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

Industry observers note that in primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.

Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely newly introduced system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.

A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring.

Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

The researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.

If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

The hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.

An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?

The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely fresh systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.

In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Industry observers note that under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

Sources indicate that the result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

#194870. How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)

How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game.
  • Sources indicate that election season can make the news feel unusually personal.
  • There is even a name for this experience: election stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game. A few minutes later, you have read three election headlines, watched a clip from a debate, skimmed dozens of comments, and somehow learned that democracy, the economy, your health care, and the future of the planet may all be in danger before breakfast.

If this sounds familiar, you are not alone.

Sources indicate that election season can make the news feel unusually personal. The issues on the ballot can affect our finances, health, schools, communities, and rights. At the same time, the way we now encounter political information—constantly, emotionally, and often in fragments—can leave us feeling overloaded rather than informed.

There is even a name for this experience: election stress. The Mayo Clinic describes it as the overwhelming anxiety some people feel during an election cycle. And surveys from the American Psychological Association suggest that elections have become a significant source of stress for many Americans. In the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, for example, 72% of adults remarked they were worried that the results could lead to violence, and 56% said they feared the election could mark the end of democracy in the United States.

It is understandable to feel unsettled when an election seems to carry serious consequences. But anxiety is not always a problem to get rid of; in small doses, it can direct our attention toward what matters. It may motivate us to learn, vote, volunteer, have difficult conversations, or support people affected by political decisions.

The problem begins when information meant to help us engage instead keeps our nervous systems in a constant state of alarm.

Part of election stress comes from the uncertainty it elicits. We do not know who will win, what policies will change, or how the people around us will respond. Research suggests that uncertainty itself can be stressful because people naturally want to understand and predict the environment around them. When we feel unable to do that, we may feel less safe and less in control.

In a recent development, news can intensify that uncertainty. Negative news is often more attention-grabbing than positive news, and conflict, danger, and outrage make especially compelling headlines. That does not mean journalists are intentionally trying to harm us. Reporting on threats and problems is an essential part of journalism. But a steady diet of alarming information can shape how we feel about the world, especially when it leaves little room for context, solutions, or signs of human cooperation.

In a recent development, this can create a difficult cycle. When people feel anxious, they often seek out more information in an effort to regain a sense of control. Yet the more election news they encounter—particularly news marked by uncertainty, conflict, and emotional intensity—the more anxious they may feel. Then they check again.

In other words, we may turn to the news to calm ourselves down, only to leave feeling more activated than before.

Political stress is not fresh. But the way we receive political information has changed dramatically.

Recent findings suggest that when John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon debated on television in 1960, viewers watched in a far more contained media environment. There was no endless stream of clips, reactions, memes, push notifications, and commentary arriving at every hour of the day. People could discuss the debate afterward, but they were not also carrying the debate around in their pockets.

Today, election news can follow us almost everywhere: to the grocery store line, the waiting room, the car, the dinner table, and bed. Social media makes it easier for people to participate politically and amplify voices that were once excluded from public conversation. Those are meaningful benefits. But the same technology can make political information feel impossible to put down.

It also encourages us to consume news in small, emotionally potent pieces. A headline while brushing our teeth. A video clip while waiting for coffee. A dramatic post at a stoplight. These snippets can provoke strong feelings without giving us enough context to understand the story fully.

That matters because headlines often tell us what to feel before they tell us what happened. Pew research found that five out of eight Americans (63%) said they only read news headlines rather than full news articles, specifically when scrolling through social media. When people repeatedly take in emotionally charged fragments of news, they may feel a growing sense of threat while having less detailed information to guide their judgments.

Industry observers note that faced with this constant emotional demand, some people keep checking the news compulsively. Others decide they have had enough and stop paying attention altogether.

News avoidance can offer temporary relief. If every update makes you tense, angry, or helpless, closing the app may feel like self-protection. In fact, a report from the American Press Institute found that a third of Americans want to disengage from news because it feels stressful and overwhelming.

Tips for managing election stress while building a better democracy.

But avoiding news altogether comes with costs, especially during an election year. It can make it harder to participate in democratic life, understand issues that affect our communities, or distinguish reliable reporting from misinformation passed along by friends, influencers, or highly partisan accounts.

The goal, then, is not to consume more news or no news. It is to develop a healthier relationship with news: one that helps us stay informed without asking our nervous systems to be on call all day.

Sources indicate that 1. Choose a news source that includes solutions, not only problems. During stressful times, it can help to seek out reporting that does more than identify what is going wrong. Constructive journalism still covers serious problems, but it also provides context, examines solutions, and asks what people and communities can do next. This approach is not about pretending everything is fine. It is about giving readers a more complete picture: What is the problem? Who is affected? What is being tried? What can citizens realistically do? Solution-oriented reporting may be especially helpful during elections because it can replace helplessness with a more grounded sense of agency and hope for the future.

Recent findings suggest that when you choose a news source, consider asking: Does this reporting leave me better informed? Does it help me understand the problem, or does it only make me feel alarmed? Does it explain possible solutions as well as the threat?

2. Balance distressing news with inspiring media. We do not need to force ourselves to be positive about difficult realities. But we can balance the emotional weight of election coverage with media that remind us of human goodness, beauty, courage, and connection.

Research suggests that stories of kindness, moral courage, and collective care can evoke feelings such as elevation, gratitude, and hope. These emotions can broaden our view of what is possible and help us feel more connected to other people. And latest research from the University of Santa Barbara suggests that these emotions can even reduce stress.

This might mean watching a short video about neighbors helping one another after a disaster, reading a profile of local organizers working across differences, listening to music that helps you settle, or returning to a film or show that leaves you feeling more hopeful about people, or nostalgic about the past.

It has been revealed that think of this as building a more balanced media diet. Election news can be an notable part of that diet, but it should not be the only thing we feed our minds. Just as eating one healthy meal a week does not transform our physical health, one inspiring story will not undo chronic stress. Over time, though, regularly choosing media that restore us, physically and mentally, can help cultivate resilience, hope, and perspective.

3. Create boundaries around when you check the news. Finally, consider treating news less like a snack and more like a meal.

Industry observers note that snacking on news all day can mean consuming a lot without ever feeling nourished. You absorb a headline here, an alert there, and a few comments in between—but never get enough context to make sense of what you are seeing. The result can be a lot of emotional calories and very little understanding.

Instead, choose one or two intentional times to engage with the news. You might read a full article over breakfast, listen to a trusted news program on your commute, or set aside 15 minutes at lunch to review the day’s major stories. If you are prone to checking headlines compulsively, digital wellness strategies such as app limits or notification settings can make those boundaries easier to keep.

It may also help to avoid making late-night news “snacking” part of your bedtime routine. By the end of the day, our emotional and cognitive resources are often already depleted. A stream of alarming headlines can rapidly turn into doomscrolling: the repeated consumption of negative online content that leaves us more agitated and less able to sleep.

Giving news its own place in the day does not mean becoming indifferent. It means making room to take in information carefully, in context, and with enough emotional space to respond thoughtfully.

According to recent reports, election stress is real because elections matter. Feeling concerned about the future does not mean that something is wrong with you; it may mean you are paying attention.

Sources indicate that but paying attention does not require constant exposure to distress. We can choose reporting that informs and empowers us, balance difficult coverage with media that reminds us of human possibility, and set boundaries that give our minds a chance to rest.

The aim is not emotional numbness. It is becoming the kind of informed citizen who can face difficult news, stay connected to what matters, and still have enough calm and hope left to act.

Industry observers note that sophie H. Janicke, Ph.D., is a positive media psychologist working as an associate professor at Chapman University, who investigates the role that new and traditional media play in promoting and affecting character development, self-transcendent emotions (such as elevation, gratitude, and awe), prosocial behavior, and happiness.

Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
  • In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
  • “Nothing came of that,” indicates Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” indicates Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

In a recent development, but now, Brinkmann says his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

According to recent reports, long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

According to recent reports, “The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on latest findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”.

Sources indicate that the east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann claims, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

Recent findings suggest that the rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”.

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail).

Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main.

The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann notes. “That was our basis.”.

Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

Industry observers note that “It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann claims. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”.

Sources indicate that they discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”.

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674).

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3.

None of these reliefs highlighted the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

Sources indicate that the team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann notes. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann states. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Recent findings suggest that brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

According to recent reports, it is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann states. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

The card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the latest card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card says something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

The system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

Scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

The physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the major figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image shows what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

#194867. Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue.
  • Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders.
  • What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. Fresh research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to important differences in the brain's structure.

Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders.

Sources indicate that an estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

Rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

The analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

"As more people recognize how important sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," remarked Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next.".

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region.

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

In a recent development, the researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward crucial information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

According to recent reports, the affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

It has been revealed that "Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," mentioned Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments.".

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences.

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

Industry observers note that people with these conditions demonstrated changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Sources indicate that together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with new clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

Sources indicate that however, an vital question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team intends to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

What’s Crucial to Us When Making Political Decisions?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy complications.
  • It has been revealed that the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans.
  • “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” mentioned Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy complications. But a new study by UC Berkeley social scientists finds that Americans usually don’t consider the full scope of difficult issues, instead basing their opinions on mental shortcuts that sidestep complexity.

It has been revealed that the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans. While some people in the study did closely analyze a range of issues before coming to an opinion, others did a quick back-of-the-napkin tally of plusses and minuses, or even more commonly based their opinions on just one factor, the authors found.

“When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” mentioned Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak. But, he added, “we find that most of them aren’t. Most commonly, people rely on a mental shortcut, effectively deciding based on the single factor they care about most and largely ignoring the rest.”.

Industry observers note that for example, when asked to choose between two fictional U.S. Senate candidates based on age, gender, race, education, military experience, and political experience, many of the study participants would make their decision based on just one of those factors.

That doesn’t mean that people are irrational, mentioned coauthor Nidhi Banavar, a Berkeley cognitive scientist. “The kind of rationality that we define in the paper is quite different from what many humans actually do in real life,” she explained. “We have these amazing brains, but they’re not the infinite computational machines that would be necessary in order to do the kind of ‘rational’ we imagine in our paper.”.

Still, the findings have clear implications for politics and political communication. For example, Banavar stated, if a leader knows that public opinion on climate change is dominated by pocketbook concerns to the exclusion of other issues, then that single factor might weigh heavily in political advertising. Complex science issues, meanwhile, might be downplayed.

The paper, “Classifying Strategy Use in Multi-Attribute Subjective Choice: Application to Conjoint Experiments in Political Science,” was published recently in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Bansak is an associate professor of political science at UC Berkeley; Banavar is a postdoctoral researcher in political science at UC Berkeley.

It has been revealed that the foundational ideals of American democracy grew from the Enlightenment era some three centuries ago. Central to that framework was a belief that humans, being rational, are capable of governing themselves—and justified in demanding political power. A core concept has been the marketplace of ideas, a constant competition between political and policy goals, looks, and analysis that would inform citizens and help them to govern themselves.

While many eras in U.S. history feature episodes in which reason faltered, modern social scientists have detailed the ways in which cognitive bias, rational ignorance, and other behaviors short-circuit reasoning. Still, the hopeful assumption about human reasoning persists.

According to recent reports, social scientists have long studied human decision making at the aggregate level. Banavar and Bansak set out to build a latest kind of cognitive model, a complex tool that can enable researchers to see an individual’s decision making mid-process, in detail.

The model doesn’t give them a view into the minds of their research subjects, but the researchers can study hundreds or thousands of decisions by an individual; from these patterns, they can perceive the values and reasoning processes that shape their decisions.

In all, nearly 3,800 people were involved in the study. Each participant sat at a computer screen, and the computer generated a random set of choices in three areas: which migrants they would rather admit to the United States, which Senate primary candidate they would rather vote for, and which climate policy package they would prefer the United States to adopt.

In a recent development, consider the basic question comparing two hypothetical migrants to the U.S. Their profiles appeared side by side, each described by six factors: region of origin, education level, gender, age, English proficiency, and whether they were seeking economic opportunity or asylum. The research subject would have to choose which of the migrants they preferred to admit to the U.S.

It has been revealed that the computer randomly presented 30 different sets of hypothetical migrants. If a participant consistently chose the younger migrant or the migrant with greater English skills, for example, the researchers could conclude that that was the most key factor for that participant.

It has been revealed that the same decision framework was presented for comparing potential climate change policies and fictional U.S. Senate candidates.

Sources indicate that the research did yield some insights about basic priorities: Participants preferred younger political candidates. They preferred climate change policy that minimized economic impact on their household. They preferred immigrants who were seeking asylum as opposed to seeking economic opportunity, and those who were below retirement age.

But that wasn’t the primary purpose of the study. Banavar and Bansak were less interested in what participants decided, and more interested in how they decided.

The results were striking: In 68% of the cases, study participants used shortcuts and did not deeply assess all six factors when choosing between hypothetical Senate candidates, migrants, or climate policies.

Industry observers note that nearly 54% showed a pattern of making choices dominated by one of the six factors. Another 14% took a different shortcut: Given six factors for each candidate or policy, they counted the total number of factors that they preferred for each, then chose the one containing the greater number.

In a recent development, how many used a comprehensive evaluation of all six factors—a rational assessment, without any shortcuts? Just under 30%.

Interestingly, Banavar mentioned, a majority of participants did not consistently stay with the same strategy. Some might rely on just one factor in choosing a climate policy, while more fully weighing all the factors in deciding which migrant to admit.

Recent findings suggest that “You can’t put people into buckets to say, ‘OK, this is someone who’s actually only going to care about only one thing,’” she said. “People are actually relating differently to each of these different domains and choosing to use different levels of effort, for want of a better term.”.

To understand why people shift strategies will require further research, she mentioned.

Industry observers note that the study comes with some notable caveats: If a participant favored female candidates, for example, or migrants who were seeking political asylum, and if both choices had those attributes, the participants had to consider other factors. That reduced, but did not eliminate, the pattern of making a choice based on one factor.

But when the researchers asked the participants to rate each profile before choosing one of them, the participants were more inclined to consider all factors in making their choices.

It has been revealed that further, the researchers allowed for only two attributes in their comparisons—male or female, for example, white or Black, or aged in their 50s or 70s. That’s not ideal, Banavar remarked, but to include multiple races, for example, is too complex for the cognitive model, and would dilute the patterns in the data. In the choice of Senate candidates, the study did not include the fictional candidates’ political parties. That question could provoke such strong, reflexive reactions that it would cloud the findings, she said.

The authors say their research has crucial implications not just for cognitive research, but for real-world, on-the-ground U.S. political processes.

Often, Bansak mentioned, our understanding of public opinion is based on surveys that ask people to choose between complex options defined by many factors. The fresh research shows analysts that individuals often base their opinions on a single factor, and that can create a clearer picture of what people want in public policy, and why they want it.

“This bears directly on how we interpret the kind of public-opinion and preference data that routinely informs policy debates and news coverage,” he noted.

And that understanding, Banavar mentioned, can shape the policy process—and political communication. If leaders present challenges in layers of complexity, “how much are people going to read or listen to that?” she asked. “What is the thing that’s really important to them, given a particular matter? That’s completely lost when you don’t think about the decision-making process.”.

Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A latest study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells.
  • According to recent reports, the research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience, found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form latest connections and helps those connections mature.
  • Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A latest study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations.

According to recent reports, the research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience, found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form latest connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons.

Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug.

The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions.

The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress.

"I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," remarked senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.

Why Scientists Are Taking a Fresh Look at Psychedelics.

Industry observers note that scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood.

It has been revealed that early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances.

In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function.

Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons.

This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions.

In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs.".

Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed.

Sources indicate that as regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer.

Watching Psilocybin Rewire the Brain.

To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy.

Industry observers note that this technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment.

Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate.

Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain.

Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines.

Recent findings suggest that but the drug did more than encourage upcoming connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace.

Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections.

Industry observers note that after psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons.

Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood.

For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin.

Sources indicate that "Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab.

"These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain.".

Psilocybin Affects Healthy and Stressed Brains Differently.

One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress.

In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level.

This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance.

The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress.

To investigate this, they used an unpredictable mild stress model, which exposes animals to varying low-intensity stressors and produces changes that resemble certain features of human depression.

Prolonged stress is known to interfere with neural communication and can cause substantial losses of synaptic connections. Over time, these changes can weaken the circuits involved in important brain functions.

When the stressed mice received psilocybin, the researchers observed an especially strong increase in the formation of fresh dendritic spines.

At the same time, psilocybin prevented the unusually high rate of connection loss associated with chronic stress.

Together, these effects suggest that psilocybin may do more than temporarily increase the number of connections in the brain. Under stressful conditions, it may also help preserve existing connections and restore circuitry that has been disrupted.

"These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain's underlying condition," Zuo added.

"This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders.".

Could Psilocybin Rewire the Brain Without Hallucinations?

Perhaps the most significant implication of the research concerns a longstanding question in psychedelic medicine: Are hallucinations and altered states of consciousness necessary for the brain changes that might contribute to therapeutic benefits?

Industry observers note that to explore this possibility, the scientists examined the role of serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs), which are proteins on the surfaces of cells that respond to chemical signals. These receptors are central to the effects of psilocybin and other classic psychedelics.

In a recent development, the researchers focused on a group of nerve cells called Layer 5 pyramidal neurons. These cells are located in the cerebral cortex, the outer region of the brain involved in complex functions such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

According to recent reports, layer 5 pyramidal neurons serve as key communication pathways that send information from the cortex to other brain regions. They also contain high levels of serotonin 2A receptors, making them especially relevant to understanding psilocybin's effects.

Using genetically modified mice, the team selectively changed whether these neurons possessed the receptors.

The results revealed a striking separation between changes in brain connections and a behavior associated with psychedelic activity.

When the researchers restored serotonin 2A receptors only in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin was still able to stimulate the development of upcoming synapses and help stabilize them.

Surprisingly, these mice did not display the characteristic head twitch response that researchers commonly use as an indicator of psychedelic activity in rodents.

The scientists then performed the opposite experiment.

When they removed serotonin 2A receptors specifically from Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin lost its ability to stimulate the same structural growth of synapses.

However, the mice still exhibited the head twitch response.

These contrasting results demonstrate that serotonin 2A receptor signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for the structural brain changes observed in the experiments, while those same receptors are not required for the psychedelic-associated behavioral response.

In other words, the cellular pathway responsible for psilocybin's brain rewiring can be separated from the pathway responsible for this particular behavioral marker of psychedelic activity.

Because mice cannot describe subjective experiences, the head twitch response does not directly establish whether an animal is experiencing hallucinations. Nevertheless, the findings provide notable evidence that these two effects involve distinct cellular mechanisms.

A Potential Path Toward Psychedelic Treatments Without the Trip.

The discovery could have major implications for the development of future psychiatric medications.

If researchers can identify compounds that activate the brain's ability to rebuild and reorganize neural connections without triggering psychedelic effects, it may become possible to create treatments that preserve some of psilocybin's therapeutic potential while avoiding the need for patients to undergo intense altered states of consciousness.

Such medications could be easier to administer and might require less intensive clinical supervision than conventional psychedelic-assisted therapies.

"By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs," Zuo stated.

"Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects -- making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population.".

Although the results are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the same cellular mechanisms operate in humans and whether separating brain rewiring from psychedelic effects can produce effective treatments for depression, PTSD, or other psychiatric disorders.

For now, the findings provide a more detailed picture of how psilocybin changes the brain and reveal a potential strategy for harnessing its effects on neural connections without relying on the psychedelic experience itself.

The study's other UC Santa Cruz coauthors include molecular and cell biologists Jacob Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, and Ju Lu, alongside Zuo.

Funding came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging. The psilocybin used in the experiments was supplied through the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Drug Supply Program.

Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you.
  • In our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love.
  • Recent findings suggest that in our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you. Or a friend who is just there to listen without telling you what you should have done differently. We don’t tend to think of these experiences as grand declarations of love, but they leave us with a certain lingering warmth: the feeling of being loved.

In our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love. This emphasis shifts attention away from the expressions of love (i.e., loving signals). While expressions are actions we choose to take, felt love is an internal, subjective sensation that washes over us. However, how strongly it does so also depends on us: The same act of care may pass unnoticed or land as love, based on the receiver’s cognitive beliefs or state of mind. Many experiences may elicit felt love, and they occur not only in romantic settings, but when we share time with friends, receive supportive gestures from family, or even get unexpected help from strangers. We are only just beginning to uncover how people come to feel loved and whether that experience can be changed—if it can be learned, like a skill.

Recent findings suggest that in our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S. population to judge situations that would make most people feel loved. What they ranked most love-eliciting was being shown compassion in difficult times—an act that, in principle, any person could (and should) offer. Pets feeling happy to see them ranked highly for eliciting the feeling of being loved. Clearly, love, as people live it day to day, reaches past courtship and partnership.

Work like this partly drives how we measure who feels loved and when. It is common for studies to measure the experience of love as if it were a stable trait—for example, romantic attachment as a demographic indicator—but this practice obscures fundamental aspects of the lived human story. Relationship status may describe part of someone’s circumstances, but it does not tell us whether that person feels loved in their daily experience. For example, many people experience love while unattached, and many do not experience love despite being in a long-term relationship. In fact, in our studies, strong experiences of felt love are reported by participants who identify as unattached. To study felt love, we also have to ask about the experience directly.

Subjective states like felt love are inherently volatile, so studying it requires many careful observations, ideally while people are going about their daily lives. We often rely on complex research methods that focus not only on how people feel at a given time, but on the patterns of change over time and how those are shaped by our environment and affected by others. Our basic approach is simple in principle: Ask people how loved they feel at different times while they go about their lives. In two studies published in 2020, in which over 200 participants reported their felt love states a handful of times per day for several weeks, we found that people with higher levels of felt love also tended to report greater flourishing and emotional well-being.

Frequent, repeated observations also allow us to disentangle a person’s typical experience from day-to-day fluctuations. This can also reveal individual differences in how persistent daily felt love states are—a feeling can be strong and brief, or weaker but sustained. Persistence is not automatically desirable: A below-usual feeling of being loved can persist, too. Whether particular patterns directly affect well-being remains an important open question.

Recent findings suggest that to study the role of persistence, we developed custom mathematical models that include love inertia—that is, how long that warm feeling stays with us. In our recently published study, 52 participants reported how loved they felt as well as how much love they had expressed over a period of 28 days. We found that people whose felt love states were more persistent also enjoyed better mental health and indicators of well-being. Even more interestingly, the more people expressed love to others in their daily lives, the more they themselves tended to feel loved in return. Expressing love appears to be a gift that keeps on giving: Showing love is associated with a lasting sense of warmth and better well-being, and it also spreads love around you.

This finding suggests an actionable insight: Expressing love could be one route to feeling loved. If you are feeling a lack of connection, proactively expressing selfless care for someone else might help jumpstart your own feelings of being loved. We don’t yet know what accounts for this association. Expressing love might invite a warm response, change how you interpret a relationship, or be part of an interaction that lifts both people up.

Can an interaction actually change how loved someone feels? A 2024 study with 218 parent–child pairs argues just that. The authors of that study randomly assigned parents and their children, aged eight to 13, to one of two nine-minute conversations. In one condition, they took turns answering questions that encouraged personal disclosure (for example, instead of a surface-level question like “How was school?,” they might ask, “What is something you worry about?”). In the other condition, they made small talk. Children in the disclosure condition reported feeling more loved during the conversation.

Industry observers note that this result cannot readily be explained by children in warmer families simply choosing more personal conversations—assignment of children to conditions was random. The researchers changed the conversation and observed a direct difference in the children’s experience.

According to recent reports, such findings need to be independently replicated for reliability and generalizability, but this is an crucial and promising step: A straightforward intervention changed an experience of feeling loved. The next question we can work on is whether changes of this kind can become part of daily life.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Our focus on the receiver side of love brings a slightly more complex perspective: that an act does not produce a loving feeling by itself, but that effect is moderated by interpretation and expectation—thoughts that come to us in the moment, cognitive beliefs that support those thoughts, and the justifications we have for those beliefs. A colleague’s quiet help can be experienced as love, or dismissed as routine professional courtesy.

It has been revealed that an area that is not yet well-explored is how the reception of expressions of love can be taught. If feelings follow perceptions, and perceptions follow beliefs, then felt love is a cognitive phenomenon in addition to an emotional one, so that cognitive skills contribute to how we experience the social world. It may be possible for people to learn to notice when they reflexively dismiss acts of care, to check their interpretation against what actually happened, and to re-evaluate in order to let the sender’s kindness count. It is also possible that a deficit in this cognitive skill prohibits many people from benefiting from the ambient love that is already present in everyday life. Even so, biased perceptions can have positive effects in this context. People with a stronger general tendency to interpret daily life experiences as expressions of love feel more loved in general, with all the well-being benefits that brings.

It has been revealed that we now have ways to measure felt love in daily life, evidence linking it to well-being, and at least one experiment that changed it in the moment. A sensible next step is to connect those findings.

In a recent development, can an intervention change daily feelings of love for weeks or months? Does that change lead to better well-being? Does it work for people who start out feeling relatively unloved, or mainly for those already doing well? Those are different questions, all embedded in the vastly complex network of our daily environments and experiences—part of what is sometimes called the exposome—and they require different, carefully drawn comparisons.

It has been revealed that future trials could focus on the cognitive component of felt love—whether an underlying ability to appreciate acts of love extends to other facets of life, and whether interventions should target the individual’s reasoning before focusing on their social context. Repeated measurements in daily-life settings could be used to show whether any differences generated by the intervention survive after the study session. Such trials would need to be designed with a great deal of care to establish the mechanisms of causality—a standard challenge of daily-life social psychology studies, but an especially critical one here. Establishing how to make experiences of felt love more available is an expansive but worthwhile scientific endeavor.

According to recent reports, finally, an emerging focus on love also recognizes how it is culturally and contextually bound. While certain loving gestures are found all over the world (such as helping someone in need, or empathic attention), to foster intercultural understanding, empathy, and inclusivity in diverse societies, it is vital to recognize love’s cultural variations in everyday life. We are currently conducting global cross-cultural research to identify specific ways love is shown in everyday life across different types of relationships, beyond just the romantic.

While we and other researchers continue to conduct larger studies to unpack these exact mechanisms, we don’t have to wait for the data to start paying closer attention to the quiet moments in our own lives. What happens when you feel genuinely cared for? What happens when you proactively express love to someone else? Being mindful of how they respond can reveal something that checking a box to count affectionate gestures misses. Fostering these experiences doesn’t require a laboratory—it is a daily practice we can all begin right now. Showing love is a low-cost experiment we can all conduct in our own daily lives.

How Young People Are Researching Concerns That Matter to Them

💡 Key Takeaways
