📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

It has been revealed that the market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

The brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a big serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

We fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

According to recent reports, the first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

The Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

In a recent development, we used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

The tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

The photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a upcoming one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

According to recent reports, with Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

Industry observers note that collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

It has been revealed that as a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

The Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

Elisha Goldstein: A Nourishing Breath Meditation

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mindful breathing often serves as the foundation for meditation practices because your breath is always with you, wherever you are, and it can be used as an anchor to the present moment.
  • With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are.
  • For dealing with the challenges of stress and anxiety, we sometimes recommend abdominal breath­ing—breathing from the belly, rather than only into the chest—as this can be very calming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mindful breathing often serves as the foundation for meditation practices because your breath is always with you, wherever you are, and it can be used as an anchor to the present moment. In essence, all that’s involved is simply being mindful when you breathe in and out. There is no need to analyze, count, visu­alize, or manipulate the breath in any way. Just breathe normally and naturally and be aware of breathing in and out. There are a few methods you can use to focus on your breath. You can be mindful of your breath in your nose, chest, belly, or even your entire body as it breathes in and out.

With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are.

For dealing with the challenges of stress and anxiety, we sometimes recommend abdominal breath­ing—breathing from the belly, rather than only into the chest—as this can be very calming. However, if another location is preferable, please listen to your own wisdom. Generally speaking, abdominal or belly breathing is the way we all naturally breathe, especially when we’re lying down. To determine if you’re breathing from your abdomen, place your hand on your belly and feel whether it expands as you inhale and contracts as you exhale. If it doesn’t, turn your attention to breathing more deeply and feeling your belly expand and contract with your breath.

An important benefit of abdominal or belly breathing is that it helps moderate irregular breathing patterns, which often arise due to stress or irritation. Anxiety can lead to shallow, rapid, or sporadic breathing and even hyperventilation, and a full-blown panic attack can cause increased shortness of breath, thoughts of losing control, and pains in the chest. By bringing the breath back into the belly, you can help the body return to balance. So when anxiety arises, first acknowledge the feeling, then gently bring attention to the abdomen and practice mindful belly breathing.

In a recent development, before we begin, we have one final bit of advice: With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This might mean simply noticing and acknowledging stress or anxiety rather than falling into old patterns of running away from it. You may discover that by embracing your fear you find your heart.

According to recent reports, do this practice in a relaxing environment without distractions, such as the phone. You can do it either lying down or sitting up, but if you lie down and find yourself falling asleep, try a more upright posture. Bring your full, undivided attention to this practice as you listen or read the following meditation, pausing after each paragraph. You can practice anytime throughout the day, combining this practice with the mindful check-in if you like.

Industry observers note that read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.

Industry observers note that elisha Goldstein, Ph.D., is a clinical psychologist and conducts a private practice in West Los Angeles. He is founder of the Mindful Living Collective—a donation-based leading global network for mindful living and learning, and creator of the Uncover the Power Within coaching program and the free master class on the Uncover the Power Within Blueprint. He is also the author of Uncovering Happiness: Overcoming Depression with Mindfulness and Self-Compassion (Atria Books, 2015), The Now Effect (Atria Books, 2012), Mindfulness Meditations for the Anxious Traveler (Atria Books, 2013), and co-author of A Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Workbook (New Harbinger, 2010).

Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for Dezeen's 20x20 project

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler.
  • The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.
  • “I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

According to recent reports, the duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Substantial Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

“We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

Humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” mentioned Bergh.

Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

Recent findings suggest that “But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” remarked Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most key thing,” she continued.

“Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

The hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

According to recent reports, “The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

“You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” remarked Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo remarked funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

“All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

Sources indicate that “It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” noted Bergh. “We have plans for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

Sources indicate that “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party.
  • Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions.
  • Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most crucial artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a new dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most important museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a new institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)Hungarian National GallerySzent György térIn Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

Working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s newly introduced Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

In a recent development, museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

Left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

Recent findings suggest that the Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

Industry observers note that A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most vital artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

Industry observers note that judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareGoya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.

An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)Id. Antall József rkpIn the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

Sources indicate that comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939).

© Museum of Fine Arts – Vasarely Museum, Budapest.

Sources indicate that victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)Vasarely Museum BudapestSzentlélek térFor the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Recent findings suggest that schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Industry observers note that pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ Square.

Hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.

Industry observers note that A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996).

Photo © József Rosta / Ludwig Museum - MoCA, Budapest.

© SUMUS Gáyor & Maurer Foundation.

In a recent development, dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)Ludwig MuseumKomor Marcell utcaDuring the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.

Recent findings suggest that A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

How to Be Grateful for Your Morning Cup of Coffee

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we’re used to saying a quick “thank you,” to the barista who serves us coffee, or the kind stranger who holds the door open as we leave the cafe.
  • That’s a concept writer AJ Jacobs explores in his TED Talk and latest book, Thanks a Thousand, based on his journey to thank everyone involved in getting that daily cup of joe into his hands.
  • While Jacobs initially believed his choice to focus on a cup of coffee would be a simple task, he soon learned that there were hundreds of people involved in producing the hot drink most of us take for granted every day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we’re used to saying a quick “thank you,” to the barista who serves us coffee, or the kind stranger who holds the door open as we leave the cafe. But how many people would you have to thank if you wanted to express gratitude to absolutely everyone responsible for your morning cup of coffee?

That’s a concept writer AJ Jacobs explores in his TED Talk and latest book, Thanks a Thousand, based on his journey to thank everyone involved in getting that daily cup of joe into his hands.

While Jacobs initially believed his choice to focus on a cup of coffee would be a simple task, he soon learned that there were hundreds of people involved in producing the hot drink most of us take for granted every day.

According to recent reports, “I would thank the trucker who drove the coffee beans to the coffee shop, but he couldn’t have done his job without the road. So I would thank the people who paved the road, and then I would thank the people who made the asphalt for the pavement,” Jacobs states. “And I came to realize that my coffee, like so much else in the world, requires the combined work of a shocking number of people from all walks of life.”.

Recent findings suggest that why bother practicing gratitude in the first place? Jacobs, like many of us, found he often overlooked the positive aspects of his day and focused on the bad. By expressing gratitude when things went right, he was able to break out of his negative thoughts.

He explains: “It allowed me to focus on the hundreds of things that go right every day, as opposed to the three or four that go wrong.”.

Here are five lessons he learned when he set out to thank everyone responsible for his morning pick me up:.

In a recent development, even if you start and end your gratitude journey by thanking your local barista (or local grocer, taxi driver, bartender, etc.) there’s a right way to do so. Namely: Look up from your phone and make eye contact.

“It reminds you, you’re dealing with a human being who has family and aspirations and embarrassing high school memories,” Jacobs claims.

Taking a moment to connect with the person serving us can help us appreciate the people we interact with daily and show them that they are not “human vending machines.”.

“That little moment of connection is so key to both people’s humanity and happiness,” Jacobs says.

As part of his mission to thank everyone, Jacobs reached out to Ed Kaufmann, who tests, tastes and selects coffee for a living. Jacobs was wowed by Kaufmann’s ability to notice all the small elements of flavor in coffee (notes of honeysuckle, for example) that most of us miss.

In our rush to finish our drink while getting ready for work, riding the subway, or taking notes in an office meeting, we often fail to slow down and truly notice what we’re tasting.

In a recent development, “Inspired by Ed, I decided to really let the coffee sit on my tongue for five seconds,” Jacobs indicates. “We’re all busy, but I could spare five seconds, and really think about the texture and the acidity and the sweetness.”.

Doing so taught Jacobs the importance of savoring—the art of slowing down rather than consuming on autopilot.

“This idea of savoring is so crucial to gratitude,” he says. “Psychologists talk about how gratitude is about taking a moment and holding on to it as long as possible, and slowing down time so that life doesn’t go by in one big blur, as it often does.”.

Sources indicate that when you consider all that goes into a cup of coffee—the beans, the sugar, the milk—it’s easy to overlook the cup itself. Yet Jacobs says one of the best conversations he had throughout his project was with a man who creates coffee cup lids.

Recent findings suggest that “He says a bad lid can ruin your coffee,” Jacobs recounts. “That it can block the aroma, which is so important to the experience. It made me realize there are hundreds of masterpieces all around us that we totally take for granted.”.

By taking the time to notice the little things we can “tap into that sense of wonder and enrich our lives,” Jacobs states.

Once he began his gratitude journey, Jacobs realized his project of writing thank you notes each day was creating a larger shift in his life: that when he saw the impact that “thank you” had on others, it began to affect him as well.

If you act as if you’re grateful, you eventually become grateful for real.

But that process often started with a lot of grumpiness and not a small amount of toil.

“I would wake up every morning in my default mood, which is grumpiness, but I would force myself to write a thank-you note, and then another, and then another,” he explains.

Despite not feeling grateful at first, Jacobs forced himself to go through the actions of gratitude and eventually noticed a transformation in his “default mood.”.

Industry observers note that “What I found was that if you act as if you’re grateful, you eventually become grateful for real,” says Jacobs. “The power of our actions to change our mind is astounding. So often we think that thought changes behavior, but behavior very often changes our thought.”.

For every one person Jacobs thanked, he learned there were many others he owed his gratitude to, people he would never be able to meet. It made him realize that sometimes, the best way to express gratitude for someone’s help is to help others in return.

“Some people worry that gratitude has a downside,” Jacobs notes. “That we’ll be so grateful, that we’ll be complacent…Well, it turns out, the opposite is true. The research demonstrates that the more grateful you are, the more likely you are to help others.”.

For example, thanking the people whose job it is to provide clean water (essential to making coffee), caused him become involved with an organization called Dispensers for Safe Water whose mission is to provide drinking water to those in need.

It has been revealed that “When you’re in a bad state, you’re often more focused on your own needs. But gratitude makes you want to pay it forward,” Jacobs concludes.

Nicole Bayes-Fleming holds an MSc in Gender, Media and Culture from the London School of Economics, where she researched the relationship between social media, knowledge production, and feminist social justice movements.

She has a bachelor’s in journalism, and has formerly worked as a digital editor and freelance reporter with bylines in Mindful Magazine, the Globe and Mail, FLARE, Ottawa Citizen, Ottawa Magazine, and HalifaxToday.ca.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

The mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

Recent findings suggest that the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

In a recent development, spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

Sources indicate that the identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron claims the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Industry observers note that saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert newly introduced audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz says the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

In 2022, Émily Adam and Jean-Christophe Lirette took over the reins from Ashton Leblond, with a vision of expanding the 23 locations of this beloved Quebec brand.

According to recent reports, the upcoming owners faced some major challenges: stagnant sales figures, outdated restaurants, an aging clientele and the need to recruit younger workers. It quickly became clear that Ashton’s brand image and experience needed to be revitalized.

LG2 reimagined Ashton’s entire brand experience at one of its flagship restaurants. Numerous elements were redesigned to simplify the brand as a whole and turn it into an exportable entity.

The experience was updated with a perfect blend of modernity and traditions rooted in Ashton’s history. In tribute to snack bar culture, all the classic codes of diners were integrated with a modern twist. A customized typographic signature emphasizing the generous, indulgent nature of Ashton dishes was created, and the chain’s signature red colour was updated. A touch of nostalgia can be felt in the fresh brand merchandise, which features illustrations reminiscent of one of Ashton’s earliest logos.

The colours are rich, curved edges are prominent and the triple red line – inspired by the chain’s iconic neon lighting – runs through every touchpoint in the graphic system, from the newly introduced packaging to the stripes on socks.

To create an atmosphere as comforting as its food, the design concept was completely overhauled. This transformation can be seen from the outer shell to the interior details: the pervasive curves, neon lighting and red tin roof are all reminiscent of Ashton’s original 1969 food truck.

It has been revealed that A monochrome red border runs through the dining room where the famous banquettes are still featured prominently in the centre. This easily reproducible layout will be extended to the chain’s other restaurants over the next few years.

35% increase in traffic at the first renovated location 34% increase in sales at the first renovated location 40% increase in visits to the Ashton website.

  • Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.
  • This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

Sources indicate that “The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”.

Sources indicate that “It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • Recent findings suggest that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers said that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

Recent findings suggest that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for big works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” noted Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a latest buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

Recent findings suggest that in the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

Subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” said the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

With India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox noted this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

Recent findings suggest that also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that revealed at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (New York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

Several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read stated that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

By and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which indicated small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

According to recent reports, while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff noted she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

Recent findings suggest that the gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff noted.

It has been revealed that speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery highlighted a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he said.

It has been revealed that the gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

Recent findings suggest that as many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," notes the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Recent findings suggest that further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan stated, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

According to recent reports, meanwhile, issues of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

India's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of latest Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

Letting the Film Breathe: A Conversation with Filmmaker Julie Bayer Salzman

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala.
  • Sources indicate that just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span.
  • In a recent development, former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala. She was so struck that she signed up for the same mindfulness course his school used to train its teachers. During one of her meditations, she pictured a short film. That film became Just Breathe, in which elementary school kids describe how mindfulness helps them work with anger. It was featured on Oprah’s Super Soul Sunday and has since been translated into six languages and shown in classrooms around the world.

Sources indicate that just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span. The five films so far cover anger in childhood, anxiety in middle school, depression in high school, addiction in midlife, and grief in the elder years. Made with her husband and creative partner, cinematographer Josh Salzman, through their company Wavecrest Films, the series is funded by donations and offered free to anyone who needs it.

In a recent development, former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024. After the recent release of Bayer’s latest film, Broken & Beautiful, Mindful Chief Editor Siri Myhrom caught up with her at her home in LA. They spoke about what it’s like to work on creative projects with her partner, what advertising taught her, how her practice reveals up on set, and what she’s learned from the people at the heart of her newest films.

Industry observers note that siri Myhrom: You spent more than a decade producing commercial campaigns before directing your own work. What did advertising teach you about storytelling, and what did you have to unlearn?

Sources indicate that julie Bayer Salzman: Advertising taught me the importance of strong visuals in nonfiction filmmaking. Sometimes documentary filmmakers don’t place as much value on the visual style as they do on simply capturing the action unfolding in order to tell the best story, and of course that makes a lot of sense in some respect, because story is everything; however, film is a visual medium, and a documentary needs to be more than journalistic. It’s worth taking time to capture reality as beautifully as you can. That remarked, sometimes when documentaries look too slick, it can be a distraction. To me it’s important to find the balance.

We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet?

Commercials also taught me how to distill a story to its essence in a short amount of time. And yet, taken too far, that can be a detriment to any story. I had to unlearn to some extent the tendency to truncate a scene out of learned impatience, or playing into the audience’s short attention span. I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but there is not a lot of breathing space in a commercial!

In a recent development, this may seem corny or cliché, but when I started practicing mindfulness, I actually started to lean more into the idea of allowing a film to breathe. As I was learning to breathe more consciously myself, my filmmaking style started to evolve differently, more experientially—slowing the pace, and allowing more pauses between the thoughts or statements.

In a recent development, SM: Wavecrest’s mission is to make content with a positive social impact, and you’ve stated you choose projects carefully so you don’t add to the noise. How do you decide whether a project is worth making?

JBS: We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet? Meaning: Does the project help us evolve collectively? Change the way we see the world? Inspire us to be better humans? Cultivate connection with nature or other humans? Laugh? If none of those things, then we’ll pass, thanks.

Recent findings suggest that SM: You and Josh are married as well as creative partners. How do you divide the work, and how do you handle creative disagreements?

JBS: We’re incredibly lucky to have very complementary skill sets, while often sharing feelings as well as values. I’m big-picture; he’s details. I’ve got a million ideas and my antennae up at all times, taking in everything around me. I “see” the film conceptually, and have my producer skill set from years in commercials, therefore I tend to take the lead as director and producer; but he’s the cinematographer, and I trust him implicitly to capture my vision in the best possible way.

I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

According to recent reports, when it’s time to edit, I lay out the story, then pass it to him to sculpt the fine details that I usually have no patience for, like on which exact frame to place a cut. He enjoys tedium in a way I don’t.

I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

SM: When did mindfulness become part of your personal life, and when did you realize it could be the subject of your films?

Sources indicate that JBS: Mindfulness became part of my life when my son started kindergarten in 2013. He came home at the age of five, talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala, thanks to the social-emotional learning curriculum at his school, and I immediately enrolled in the course that the school’s principal used to train the teachers. While meditating one day, I envisioned the first film in the Mindful Shorts series, Just Breathe, and promptly made that film. Once I saw the success it was having, I realized that people were hungry for this type of learning, and the rest of the series evolved from there.

Sources indicate that SM: You describe the Mindful Shorts as “experiential” films. What does that mean to you, and how do you design a film that viewers experience rather than just watch?

JBS: It means artfully crafting a film that results more in an embodied experience for the audience, rather than a passive viewing. We don’t conform to traditional standards in order to tell a story; we shape it in such a way that we hope the viewers walk away from the film feeling different energetically than they did at the start. That there is an actual impact on the nervous system—a sense of calm, of understanding—a certain kind of peace within.

In a recent development, when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers.

SM: Does your own mindfulness practice change how you behave on set, such as how you listen, when you stay quiet, or how you handle the unexpected?

JBS: Absolutely. The quality of presence, of attention, are much greater now. I’m far less in my head than I used to be, and it allows for more spontaneity and creative problem solving. I think my practice allows me to be much more fluid and present than I used to be.

In a recent development, when I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers. The goal is not to cross items off a list; it’s to have an experience with the process itself.

Recent findings suggest that SM: Mindfulness is an inner experience, and film is a visual medium. How do you show something that happens inside a person?

JBS: When you’re talking about something in one’s interior world, the exterior world must match it. Yes, film itself is a visual medium, but filmmaking as an art form is multisensory. In addition to having a distinct visual style, we place an enormous value on sound—ambient noise, music, everything—as well as on editorial pacing. It all must reflect the emotional tone behind what is being said, the changes and transformation that a character is going through when they are learning how to mindfully show up in the world.

We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature.

Industry observers note that SM: Your films are unscripted and often feature people talking about very personal struggles. How do you create the kind of safety and trust that lets people be that open on camera?

In a recent development, JBS: I’m not sure I can answer this question, because it’s not something I consciously do. I think it’s mostly inherent to who both Josh and I are as human beings. We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature. I like to think that people just instinctively trust that we are safe to be vulnerable with, that we emanate an air of security.

SM: The series follows mindfulness from childhood through old age, moving from anger, to anxiety, depression, addiction, and grief. Was that structure planned from the beginning, or did it develop as you went?

JBS: Both. After the success of Just Breathe (on anger and elementary school kids), I recognized there was more work to be done. I awoke at 3 a.m., seeing the rest of the series in my head, so I grabbed my journal, sat on the couch, and wrote the progression of the films in a way that made sense to me.

Sources indicate that what’s after elementary school? Middle school, when we start to name “stress.” I immediately thought about how people tend to project their anxieties on the world around them, and decided we had to project images on our subjects for that film (which eventually became Release). And then I started to think about high school, when we start to name “Depression,” and I began conjuring up what that film (Into Light) might look like. Next I started to think about the stage of middle life, when addiction tends to surface and become a problem for many. And on and on…it was a middle-of-the-night revelation of sorts.

The two most recent Mindful Shorts carry the series into adulthood. A Good Day (32 minutes) explores mindfulness and addiction in midlife, and won at the Real HeArt Film Festival. Broken & Beautiful (23 minutes) centers on Sandy Phillips, who turned to mindfulness after the death of her daughter, and took top honors at LA Shorts.

SM: A Good Day takes on addiction in midlife and is the longest Mindful Short so far. Why did this subject need more time than the earlier films?

It has been revealed that JBS: Addiction is often the result of the unprocessed experiences that the earlier films delve into (anger, anxiety, depression, and trauma), and it’s something we don’t often deal with until we’re middle aged, so as I was editing the film, I felt the need to go deeper into it, covering ground I thought was necessary in order to be more comprehensive, which naturally resulted in a longer film. I guess it’s fair to say that the topic itself seemed to dictate the length of the film.

When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses.

Industry observers note that SM: Broken & Beautiful is about a particular kind of grief, the terrible loss of a child, and, more generally, grief in the elder years. What did you learn from older subjects about presence and loss that younger subjects couldn’t have taught you?

It has been revealed that JBS: When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses. The subject of Broken & Beautiful, Sandy Phillips, possesses a certain wisdom that only comes with age. That’s not to say that someone younger couldn’t speak to loss or grief, but she has lived through so much—and she started practicing mindfulness specifically to help herself process and navigate the death of her daughter.

That kind of perspective is rarely inherent in any one person’s being; it takes real time and intention to cultivate and embody it. Her particular quality of presence and attention is something that is earned, and learned, over years.

SM: Did making Broken & Beautiful affect how you deal with grief in your own life?

Sources indicate that JBS: I think it impacted Josh more than me so far, as he had to deal with the unexpected death of his mother from a heart attack in 2012—a trauma that took him a long time to process. I think I can speak for him, though, when I say he no longer sees death as an ending to a person or the relationship with that person—something that was very difficult for him to accept earlier.

And then, sadly and tragically, the young kintsugi artist in Broken & Beautiful, Fumika Tanokashira, died suddenly last spring (2026), and I’m not sure I can quite put my finger on it but there was something profound about it all—the fact that she is the one showing us metaphorically, via kintsugi, how to put our lives back together after a terrible loss, and here she is the one now gone. It just leaves me speechless every time I think about it.

For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why.

SM: Your next film is about trauma in young adults and will focus on the science behind mindfulness. Why add a scientific angle now, and how do you strategy to balance research with personal stories?

JBS: I haven’t been awoken by a vision for that one yet! But I trust it will come…it always does. Sometimes it’s imagined ahead of time; sometimes it just emerges organically during the process of making a film. We shall see what the future holds.

It has been revealed that but to answer the question of “why add a scientific angle now”: because skeptics still exist. For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why. Proof must be in the data. Well, there’s plenty of data out there, and I intend to do something with it. I just have to find the right people who wish to collaborate on making that film. I know they’re out there.

SM: The Mindful Shorts are funded through donations and offered for free. What does that model make possible, and what does it make harder?

JBS: What the model makes possible is grant money, because the series is produced as not-for-profit. We also retain full ownership and creative control of the content. There’s a certain satisfaction in knowing that anyone who needs the films can access them for free, even if it takes years to find them!

Yet the downside of that all is that we don’t have access to “investor” money. Investors want to know they’ll get their money back and more (spoiler alert: they won’t). It’s also harder to get third-party distribution when you go the not-for-profit model, so we self-distribute on YouTube, Vimeo, and other social media platforms (as well as of course have the films up on our website, Wavecrest Films). It’s certainly not the most lucrative way of doing things, but it feels right given the nature of what we’re trying to do.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer.

Sources indicate that SM: You’ve urged your audience to work on being better humans because the planet demands it. How do your environmental work and your mindfulness work connect for you?

JBS: Our first film, Time & Tide (2006), was on climate change in the South Pacific, and for years afterward, the environment was top on our list of topics we felt we, as filmmakers, must address. But then I started to think that there was no point trying to convince people to change their actions without teaching them first about self-awareness.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer. We have to heal ourselves first if we wish to heal the planet. I do firmly believe though that once there’s a larger sea change of consciousness, planetary health will improve—one person at a time.

Siri Liv Myhrom is a writer, editor, and certified spiritual director from Minneapolis, MN, where she has lived with her husband and two young daughters for 20 years. Her meditation practices include cycling, cold dipping in the nearby lake, and playing the ukulele (low skill but lots of gusto). She is the Editor at Mindful.

WHEN
