📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, claims: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a newly introduced national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, says the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

Industry observers note that charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he notes. “The biggest issue seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

In a recent development, the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report states.

UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, indicates: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a upcoming Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

pen.dev: The Fast Agentic Canvas in Our Daily Workflow

💡 Key Takeaways
  • pen.dev pairs a 60fps WebGL canvas and live shaders with browser import and two-way MCP integration for real product design.
  • We've been testing pen.dev closely for quite some time, and we're ready to say it: for our daily work at Abduzeedo, it has gotten our full attention and replaced Figma in our day-to-day flow.
  • It has been revealed that the speed is truly impressive, and that speed helps you ideate more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

pen.dev pairs a 60fps WebGL canvas and live shaders with browser import and two-way MCP integration for real product design.

We've been testing pen.dev closely for quite some time, and we're ready to say it: for our daily work at Abduzeedo, it has gotten our full attention and replaced Figma in our day-to-day flow. That isn't a claim we make lightly. pen.dev feels like the closest we get to designing the real product. For anyone who spends a lot of time in the browser inspector or has been coding in the past, the whole environment feels immediately familiar.

It has been revealed that the speed is truly impressive, and that speed helps you ideate more. Built on a custom WebGL renderer, the canvas stays locked at 60fps even when you throw 10,000 photos and 10GB of content at it. Panning, zooming, and nudging dense artboards feel instant, with none of the sluggishness that slows down exploration.

According to recent reports, what makes pen.dev feel like a real design tool rather than a prompt box is how much hands-on visual control you keep. You get a proper pen tool, flex layout, variables, snapping, and familiar shortcuts, alongside components with overrides and slots plus shared design systems that make it easy to manage your workflows and keep every project in sync across files. Real-time shaders, linear, radial, angular, and mesh gradients, and masking sit right inside the inspector. Having live shaders built directly into the canvas changes how promptly you can test atmosphere and depth without jumping to another app.

Recent findings suggest that iterating with multiple agents is where the workflow really opens up. Instead of waiting on one linear prompt thread, you can spin up parallel agents to generate side-by-side variants right on the canvas and test completely different concepts at the same time. In the Goodies view, you can see directions like Darkmatter, Brickworks, and Verdant Ark laid out next to each other as real, editable frames. Agents can also draw custom icons and illustrations directly on the same layers you edit by hand, leaving plenty of room for the happy accidents that only happen when you're moving rectangles around yourself.

One of our favorite features is importing directly from the browser. In the age of AI, design more than ever is a two-way street. Sometimes you don't start from the design tool at all, you start from a working prototype or a live site. Being able to pull that straight into pen.dev for quick visual iterations is often way quicker and cheaper than trying to explain every tweak to an AI in words. For those of us who sometimes have a hard time translating ideas into prompts, but not into visuals, that completes the loop.

You can also pull 10 to 15 live reference sites onto the canvas in a grid, or keep your running localhost app open in a split-screen browser right beside its source design to compare spacing and typography in real time.

Where things really click for us is the two-way MCP integration. Inside the settings panel, you can wire up external MCP servers like Linear, Notion, or Mobbin so agents on the canvas pull real product specs and UI references as you design. Going the other way, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity connect to pen.dev over MCP to read your frames directly.

It has been revealed that because every project saves as an open .pen JSON file right inside your repository, coding agents build from your actual components, spacing, and variables instead of guessing from a flat screenshot. You can open the design and code side by side with the VS Code and Cursor extensions, run headless workflows through the pen.dev CLI, or use one-click export to HTML with CSS or Tailwind.

According to recent reports, design thinking stays on the canvas, and clean implementation follows right behind it. Explore the tool and try the web app at pen.dev.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s newly introduced function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

According to recent reports, comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “key conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

Tiffany & Co. Brings a Century of American Beauty to Crystal Bridges

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co.
  • According to recent reports, discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co.
  • In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

According to recent reports, discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that the diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the company’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

Industry observers note that an 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the organization’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

According to recent reports, bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

According to recent reports, installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

“This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” states Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

Inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

Recent findings suggest that george Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

According to recent reports, the brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

Industry observers note that george Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s New Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

In a recent development, A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

While Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Recent findings suggest that jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the firm’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”.

It has been revealed that jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

Unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

In fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

One of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

To ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

It has been revealed that because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

Sources indicate that an audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Industry observers note that ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

The more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its upcoming director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he stated he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

“The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

Industry observers note that the Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

It has been revealed that this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

But Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he says. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

According to recent reports, from one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental highlights of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he claims.

From the Finns, he will also bring an notable lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he claims: “Less talking, more doing.”.

How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, the sauna is no longer a standalone box with a stove but one stop in a longer sequence of heat, steam, snow, and ice—staged in environments built to be experienced rather than simply sat in.
  • “Traditionally, many wellness areas were centered around a single sauna or steam room.
  • Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, the sauna is no longer a standalone box with a stove but one stop in a longer sequence of heat, steam, snow, and ice—staged in environments built to be experienced rather than simply sat in. As wellness culture expands, the single hot cabin is giving way to a full hot-and-cold circuit, and Klafs’s designers focus less on guarding any one tradition than on what German engineering can do with heat, air, and materials.

“Traditionally, many wellness areas were centered around a single sauna or steam room. Today, we increasingly design complete thermal circuits where guests move intentionally between heat, cold, relaxation, and recovery stages,” according to the designers at Klafs. “This creates a more immersive experience and allows consumers to benefit from the proven physiological effects of contrast therapy.”.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

At Klafs headquarters, where the company’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a glass-enclosed sauna, just the first stop on a journey through its latest wellness innovations. Heinrich, an experienced training manager, speaks to the heater in the corner.

“Hey, Klafs,” he claims, as casually as one might address Alexa or another voice assistant. The heater is less a heat source than a host, and a smart aufguss guide signals the sauna’s evolution into a more personalized environment.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” The guided sauna ritual typically combines water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air, giving many contemporary saunas their distinctly social character.

Klafs’s Vitality Boost, billed by the company as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that communal ritual into an individual, automated experience without requiring a towel-spinning guide or the need to leave the wooden bench.

Industry observers note that blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Sources indicate that the heat is only half the circuit, and the cooling phase gets the same design attention. A full hot-and-cold circuit, the design team says, turns “a collection of individual experiences into a carefully choreographed wellness journey.” After a hot session, a bather can retreat into the chill of a Frimas ice steam room, where a sculptural central ice fountain sprouts icy, flower-like formations and a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of an ice steam shower.

It has been revealed that kept between 32 and 41 degrees Fahrenheit (0 and 5 degrees Celsius) and designed for stays of up to 10 minutes, the room aims, the company says, to help more people complete the full hot-cold-hot cycle. Glowing blue through the ice, it feels almost extraterrestrial, making the cooldown something to linger in rather than endure.

According to recent reports, klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Hot and cold areas create very different conditions, the team notes, so surfaces must withstand shifting temperatures, humidity, and heavy use. Natural stone, porcelain, thermally modified woods, and high-quality metals are commonly chosen for their durability and appearance.

Sources indicate that tactile comfort matters just as much. As guests move through a circuit, they should feel a noticeable shift in atmosphere, texture, lighting, and acoustics – cues that help them navigate the space and lead them intuitively to the next stage without extensive signage.

Other eye-catching innovations include foam steam baths, which immerse guests in suds reminiscent of childhood bubble baths. Hotels and spas can incorporate these treatments into their wellness programming as communal experiences. Klafs’s proprietary Espuro foam essence contains plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds.

Industry observers note that designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

Beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. Its retractable S1 sauna addresses the spatial constraints of residential interiors by extending from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna. Meanwhile, the S11, designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, combines delicate washi paper, multicolor light panels, and gently curved forms.

Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

With the trend toward integrating thermal wellness experiences more holistically, Klafs has also expanded into developing relaxation lounges, digital wellness guidance, and biophilic design elements.

Recent findings suggest that the circuit here feels more like traversing a wellness lab than a manufacturing facility. And the sauna itself, moving far beyond being a stop or an object, is an expanded site of possibility.

Bianca Weeko Martin is a writer and researcher whose work explores the intersection of architectural practice, theory, and personal narrative. She is the author of Architectural Guide Manila.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that in the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am right now VP of Innovation.

Sources indicate that cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

We created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

According to recent reports, next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

After our pilot study with this fresh group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

In a recent development, I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

Sources indicate that we ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

According to recent reports, all participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as issues. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of issues found included:.

Examples of suggestions included:.

Issues and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an concern is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

This site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall issues and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

It has been revealed that on this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more issues and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most concerns.

Sources indicate that here, cognitive participants found 6 more problems and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

On this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more issues and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

According to recent reports, something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more complications on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

In a recent development, the other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more concerns with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

When I grouped problems by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

Let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability challenges, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared issues and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more issues related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

In working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load complications consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

These are improvements that would give all customers more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but key concerns with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

It has been revealed that anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout swiftly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of people, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

These complications likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

The study demonstrated that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

It has been revealed that you create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability challenges start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some users.

The percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

People with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability concerns that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology people is still very notable, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation users more approachable.

It has been revealed that in this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more problems and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

It has been revealed that cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

In a recent development, this study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

Recent findings suggest that different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the matter and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

I’ve compiled a few useful resources as you begin your cognitive inclusion journey.

Tips on front-end & UX, delivered weekly in your inbox. Just the things you can actually use.

With practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A.

Everything TypeScript, with code walkthroughs and examples. And other printed books.

Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences.
  • In a recent development, in 2015, Meyohas released Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

In a recent development, in 2015, Meyohas released Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Newly introduced York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the Fresh Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

For today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her upcoming installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

It has been revealed that “The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

According to recent reports, the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she indicates. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

Recent findings suggest that that initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

Industry observers note that what began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas notes. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas notes. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, New York.

Industry observers note that neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Recent findings suggest that “Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

In a recent development, phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

#194738. 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • Sources indicate that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • Sources indicate that what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

Sources indicate that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

Sources indicate that what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

In a recent development, when I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out strategy. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

It has been revealed that we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

In a recent development, one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

In my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

According to recent reports, I’m a significant believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

Clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

Recent findings suggest that it got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to proposal? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

Industry observers note that this sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

It has been revealed that kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

My mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

My conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

Recent findings suggest that we talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

It has been revealed that in my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

Industry observers note that we’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

If you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, newly introduced perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

Industry observers note that what surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Recent findings suggest that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

In a recent development, all six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

In a recent development, caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Major Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

Tech Report: The Impact Of Humanoid Robots On Humanity

📅 2026-06-12 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

Recent findings suggest that I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

We have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

Recent findings suggest that the current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

In a recent development, what truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

According to recent reports, yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

It has been revealed that when this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

In a recent development, if you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

According to recent reports, in the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

Meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a organization called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

Industry observers note that while these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

They say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

Industry observers note that outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

In a recent development, in the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

Recent findings suggest that however, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

On the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

As humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

In a recent development, the economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very swiftly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

In a recent development, there is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

The dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

If history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

According to recent reports, the upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too significant to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

In the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

This shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

It has been revealed that as the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

It has been revealed that A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

Geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

Titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

From a sculptural glass candelabra to a beaded floor-standing candleholder, the exhibition explores the relationship between materiality, scale, and function. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

In a recent development, participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Firm, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Industrial forms mingle with playful figurative designs, including a carved wooden dog and a sculptural arrangement of flowers. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

In a recent development, candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, Newly introduced York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

Lit candles cast warm pools of light and shadows across the surrounding surfaces, bringing another dimension to the sculptural objects. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio MAJOR has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, MASSIVE designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the newly introduced district.

In a recent development, nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s latest Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,.

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a fresh development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert noted.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”.

Sources indicate that the hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

Here, projecting bays and set-back terraces will help to create privacy for the residents, whose homes will overlook a shared courtyard.

BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

SIGNIFICANT also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

#194732. Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking
